## Summary

I scanned the OAuth service (10 source files, no dependency manifest present). After tracing data flows and self-verifying, I found **3 exploitable findings**, all rooted in `String.startsWith` being misused as a URL/host trust check:

| # | Canonical ID | Severity | Sink | Root cause |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | `authentication-bypass` | CRITICAL | `verifyJwt` with attacker-fetched key | JWT `jku` header (untrusted) → `fetchKey` guard `startsWith('https://keys.example.test')` is bypassable via `keys.example.test.evil.com` / `@evil.com` userinfo + `redirect:'follow'`. Attacker signs tokens with their own key. |
| 2 | `ssrf` | HIGH | `fetch()` in `jwks.js` | Same `jku` sink + prefix guard lets the server fetch internal hosts (e.g. `https://keys.example.test@169.254.169.254/...` cloud metadata) and follow redirects. |
| 3 | `open-redirect` | HIGH | `redirect_uri` handling in `register.js` | `validateRedirect` does `redirectUri.startsWith(client.baseUrl)` — bypassable via `portal.example.test.evil.com` / `@evil.com`, enabling authorization-code/token interception. The repo's own `exact-redirect.js` (decoy) shows the correct exact-match approach. |

I deliberately did **not** report pattern-only false positives:
- `src/oauth/state.js` — uses `crypto.randomBytes(32)` + `crypto.timingSafeEqual` with length precheck (correct, no CSRF/state finding).
- `src/oauth/pkce.js` — SHA-256 verifier challenge is correct.
- `src/http/safe-jwks.js` — the *decoy*; hardcodes URL with `redirect:'manual'` (this is the safe pattern, not a finding).
- `src/logging.js` — logs only `clientId`/`outcome`, no secrets.
- `src/config.js` — only a public issuer URL + `RS256` algorithm allow-list.

I verified each bypass concretely with `new URL()` parsing in Node before reporting. The final machine-readable report is saved to `SECURITY_REVIEW.json` in the required shape (valid JSON, 3 findings, 10 scanned files, `source_modified: false`).
